idea_angle: One long-form roundup of the nine scams that peak between Black Friday and New Year, each with how it works, the tell, and the fix.

script.title: 9 holiday scams that peak before New Year (and how to beat each one)
script.hook: 9 scams peak between Black Friday and New Year. By the end of this, you'll spot every one in seconds.

segments.heading: Why the holidays
segments.narration: Between Black Friday and New Year, we buy more online, ship more packages, give to more charities, and travel more. Every one of those is a door scammers know we'll walk through, usually while we're busy and distracted. That's the whole strategy: reach you when you're rushed. So here are the nine scams that peak this season. For each one, you'll get how it works, the one tell that gives it away, and the fix. And stay to the end, because all nine share three tells, and once you know those, you'll recognise scams that aren't even on this list.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes in front of a calendar from November to January No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 1. Fake stores
segments.narration: Number one, fake online stores. They show up in social media ads with huge discounts: closing-down sales, seventy percent off everything, or a near-perfect copy of a brand you know. You pay, and either nothing arrives or a cheap knockoff does. The tell is a store you've never heard of, found through an ad, with prices far below everyone else. The fix: search the store name plus the word scam, look for a real address and phone number, and always pay with a credit card. Under federal law you can dispute a charge for something that never arrived. Payment apps and bank transfers rarely give you that.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a shop front with a crooked discount banner No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 2. Delivery texts
segments.narration: Number two, fake delivery texts. 'Your package couldn't be delivered, update your address,' with a link. With so many real packages coming, it's easy to tap. The link leads to a page asking for a small redelivery fee, and it's your card number they want. The tell: you never signed up for text updates. The Postal Service says it won't text you about a package unless you asked, with a tracking number. The fix: track packages by typing the tracking number into the carrier's own site, and forward fake texts to seven seven two six.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a parcel and a phone with a warning bubble No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 3. Gift card draining
segments.narration: Number three, gift card draining. Thieves take cards off store racks, record the numbers, cover the PIN with a new sticker, and put them back. When you load a hundred dollars, their software spends it before your gift is ever opened. The tell is packaging that's torn, re-taped, or a PIN strip that looks off. The fix: check the card, take one from the back of the rack or ask for one behind the counter, keep the receipt, and give it soon. And a related rule: anyone who asks to be paid in gift cards is a scammer.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a gift card rack with one tampered card No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 4. Charity scams
segments.narration: Number four, charity scams. Giving Tuesday and year-end appeals bring fake charities with sound-alike names, and fake 'thank you for last year's pledge' calls. The tell: pressure to give right now, on this call, or a request for gift cards, wires or crypto. The fix: look the charity up yourself, check it in the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search, and give on its own website by credit card or check. After disasters, give to established groups you already know, not pages that appeared this week.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a heart-shaped donation box with a magnifying glass No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 5. Tickets
segments.narration: Number five, ticket scams. A sold-out holiday show, and someone in a fan group, or a hacked friend's account, has two tickets at face value. They want a payment app, sent as friends and family to avoid fees. That setting usually means no purchase protection, and screenshots of tickets can be sold to ten people. The fix: buy through the venue's official resale or a platform with buyer protection, by credit card. If a friend is selling, call them, a real voice call, before you pay.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. two tickets and a phone with a payment toggle No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 6. Puppies
segments.narration: Number six, pet scams. Adorable photos, a low price, and a seller who's always too far to visit. After the deposit, the fees start: shipping, a special crate, insurance, a vet certificate, and finally 'your puppy is stuck at the airport'. There was never a puppy. The fix: reverse image search the photos, see the animal in person or on a live video call where the seller does what you ask, and never pay a stranger by gift card, payment app or wire. Better still, adopt from a local shelter you can visit.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a puppy silhouette with a ladder of price tags No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 7. Support numbers
segments.narration: Number seven, fake customer service numbers. A flight is cancelled or a package is lost, you search for the company's phone number, and the top result is an ad that goes to a scammer. Or you complain on social media and a fake support account replies, 'DM us your order number.' The fix: get support numbers only from the official app, the website you typed in yourself, or the back of your card, your statement, or your booking email. Real agents never ask for gift cards, your full password, or remote access.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a search bar with a masked phone icon No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 8. Fake invoices
segments.narration: Number eight, fake invoices. 'Your order of four ninety-nine has shipped. Didn't authorize it? Call our billing team.' There's no order. On the call, they ask for your card to process a refund, or remote access to your computer, or they fake a refund with an extra zero and ask you to send the difference back. The fix: never call the number in the email. Log in to the real account or check your card statement. No charge there means no charge.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an envelope with a fake receipt and a phone hook No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 9. Holiday romance
segments.narration: Number nine, the holiday romance. Someone met online, kind, always far away, video never works. Right before the holidays they need money for a flight home, or a gift they sent you is stuck in customs with a fee. The fix is two questions: have I met them in person or on live video, and are they asking for money? No and yes means stop. If it's a parent, start gently, 'tell me about them', because shame pushes people closer to the scammer.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a heart on a string to a distant island No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The three tells
segments.narration: So here are the three tells all nine share. One: rush. A deadline, a countdown, 'today only', 'the puppy will suffer'. Two: secrecy or isolation. Don't tell your bank, leave the app, keep it between us. Three: a strange payment. Gift cards, wires, crypto, payment apps to strangers. See two of those three, and stop. Hang up, close the tab, and check with someone you trust. Save this video, send it to the person in your family who does the holiday shopping, and follow for one scam decoded every day.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes holding up three fingers in front of a festive backdrop No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: How to protect your parents from scams: the complete guide
script.hook: 1 visit home, 5 settings, 1 conversation. Here's how to protect your parents from scams.

segments.heading: Why parents
segments.narration: Older adults are targeted more, and lose more when it happens, according to the FBI's own elder fraud reports. It's not because they're less smart. It's because they often have savings, a home, a landline that still rings, and good manners that make hanging up feel rude. Scammers also know older adults are less likely to report it, out of embarrassment. So the goal of this video isn't to scare your parents. It's to give your family a plan made calmly, in advance, so that when a scary call comes in, nobody has to think. You'll need one visit and about an hour.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes beside two simple older silhouettes No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The conversation
segments.narration: Start with the conversation, and avoid two phrases: 'you'd fall for this' and 'that's so obvious'. Instead, ask: has anyone weird called or texted lately? Almost everyone has a story, and telling it makes them the expert. Or go first: 'I almost fell for one last month.' That makes it normal. Then ask for their help: 'Help me set up a plan for the whole family, including the kids.' People follow plans they helped make. Keep it short and practical. You're not giving a lecture, you're setting up a system.
segments.on_screen_text: Start with a question, not a lecture
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. two figures at a kitchen table with coffee No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The family word
segments.narration: Step one, the family safe word. Scammers can clone a voice from a short clip online, so 'it sounded just like my grandson' is no longer proof. Pick a word or phrase that isn't on social media: not a pet's name, street, or school. Say it out loud, don't text it. The rule: anyone calling in a panic about money has to say the word. No word, or they dodge the question, and you hang up and call that person back on the number you already have. The FBI recommends exactly this.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a key inside a speech bubble No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Call-back and payment rules
segments.narration: Step two, two rules. The call-back rule: any urgent call about money, from the bank, the police, Medicare, or family, gets a hang-up and a call back on a number you look up yourself, because caller ID can be faked. The payment rule: nobody in the family pays someone who contacted them with gift cards, wires, payment apps to strangers, crypto, or cash handed to a courier. Write those two rules on a card by the phone. They beat most scams on their own.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a circular arrow and crossed-out payment icons No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Phone settings
segments.narration: Step three, the phone. While you're there, turn on the phone's built-in spam call filtering, and silence unknown callers if your parent is comfortable with that. Set an account PIN with their carrier and turn on number lock or port-out protection if offered. Update the phone's software. And look for remote access apps they didn't install on purpose; if a 'technician' put one there, remove it and change passwords. Fifteen minutes here removes a lot of scam calls before they ever ring.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a shield and toggles No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Credit freezes
segments.narration: Step four, freeze their credit at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. It's free by law, doesn't change their score, and stops anyone opening new credit in their name. Do yours at the same time, side by side, so it feels like a family task, not a judgment. Save the logins somewhere safe. If they ever need new credit, they lift one bureau for a day. And if they file taxes, get each of them an IRS Identity Protection PIN at IRS dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. three padlocks and a tax form No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Bank alerts and trusted contact
segments.narration: Step five, the bank. Turn on transaction alerts so unusual withdrawals show up right away. Ask their bank about adding a trusted contact person, someone the bank can reach if they see signs of fraud or exploitation. That person doesn't get access to the money, just a call. And agree on one family member they'll call before sending any money someone asked for, especially if they were told to keep it secret.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a bank building with a bell and a linked phone No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The fridge card
segments.narration: Then make it visible. A fridge card with large type: hang up and call back; ask for our word; never pay with gift cards, wires, payment apps or crypto; never read out a code; call this person first. Add the bank's fraud number and ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov. When someone is panicking, they won't remember a conversation from Thanksgiving, but they will see the fridge.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a fridge with a card under a magnet No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If it happens
segments.narration: And if it happens anyway, the plan is speed, not shame. Call the bank using the number on the card. Call the gift card or payment app company. Change the email password. Freeze credit. Report it at ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov and, for internet crime, I C 3 dot gov. And warn them about recovery scams: anyone offering to get the money back for a fee is the next scammer. Our printable Family Scam-Proofing Kit has all of this on paper, linked below. Send this video to your siblings, and plan the visit.
segments.on_screen_text: If it happens: speed, not shame

script.title: Identity theft recovery, step by step (what to do in the first week)
script.hook: 5 steps, 7 days. What to do when someone opens an account in your name.

segments.heading: Signs
segments.narration: It usually starts with something small. A bill for a card you never opened. A collections call about a debt that isn't yours. A letter about a loan application. Your tax return rejected because one was already filed. Or a credit alert you didn't expect. First, breathe. Identity theft is fixable, and there's a free official process for it. This video walks through the first week in five steps: confirm, contain, report, repair, and prevent. Pause it at each step and do the step.
segments.on_screen_text: Signs someone is using your identity
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes reading an unexpected letter calmly No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 1. Confirm
segments.narration: Step one, confirm what's actually happened. Pull your credit reports from all three bureaus for free at AnnualCreditReport dot com. Look for accounts, addresses, and hard inquiries you don't recognise. Check your bank and card statements for charges you didn't make. And call the company that contacted you, using a number from its official website, not the one in the letter or call. Write down everything: names, dates, account numbers. You'll need it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a magnifying glass over three simple reports No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 2. Contain
segments.narration: Step two, contain it, the same day. Freeze your credit at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion so nothing new can be opened. Call the fraud department of each company where an account was opened or misused, explain it's identity theft, and ask them to close or freeze it. Change passwords for your email and financial accounts, starting with email, because email resets everything else. If your Social Security number was used, consider an IRS Identity Protection PIN too.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. padlocks snapping shut on several doors No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Freeze vs alert
segments.narration: A quick note on freezes versus fraud alerts. A fraud alert is also free; it tells lenders to take extra steps to verify it's you. Place one at any bureau and it's passed to the others. An initial alert lasts a year; with an identity theft report you can get an extended alert for seven years. A freeze is stronger, because lenders can't pull your report at all. Many people use both.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a padlock next to a flag No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 3. Report
segments.narration: Step three, report it at IdentityTheft dot gov. It's the FTC's official site. You answer questions about what happened, and it creates an FTC Identity Theft Report plus a personalised recovery plan with pre-filled letters. That report matters: it's what you'll show businesses and the credit bureaus to get fraudulent accounts and debts removed. Some creditors may also ask for a police report; your local police can take one, bring your FTC report with you.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a simple government form with a check mark No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 4. Repair
segments.narration: Step four, repair. Send each credit bureau a dispute for every fraudulent account or inquiry, with your identity theft report. Under federal law, bureaus have to block information resulting from identity theft once you provide that report. Send letters to the companies too, asking them to close the account and confirm in writing you're not responsible. Keep copies of everything, and send important letters by certified mail. It's slow, but it works.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a stack of letters with return receipts No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Debt collectors
segments.narration: If debt collectors call about a fraudulent debt, tell them in writing that it's the result of identity theft, include your report, and ask them to stop and to tell the original creditor. Don't pay a debt that isn't yours to make the calls stop. And watch out for recovery scams: anyone who contacts you offering to fix your identity theft for a large upfront fee is likely another scammer.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a letter and a shield No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 5. Prevent
segments.narration: Step five, prevent the next one. Keep your credit frozen. Use a password manager and passkeys. Turn on alerts for every account. Check your credit reports a few times a year. Shred mail with account numbers. If you'd like someone else watching for you, identity monitoring services can alert you to new activity and help with recovery paperwork. That's optional; the freeze does the heavy lifting, and it's free.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a shield over a house with a padlock No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Confirm with your free reports. Contain it today with freezes, calls and new passwords. Report it at IdentityTheft dot gov. Repair it with disputes and letters. Prevent the next one with a freeze, a password manager and alerts. Save this video, because the person who needs it might be you, or your mom, a year from now. Follow for one scam decoded every day.

script.title: Credit freeze vs fraud alert vs monitoring: what you actually need
script.hook: 4 ways to protect your credit, 2 of them free. Here's which ones you actually need.

segments.heading: The four options
segments.narration: When people worry about identity theft, they usually hear about four things: a credit freeze, a fraud alert, a credit lock, and paid identity monitoring. They get mixed up all the time, and some ads make it sound like you need to pay for protection. You don't, for the most important part. Here's what each one actually does, what it costs, and who should use which. Full disclosure up front: we have an affiliate link for one monitoring service, and we'll still tell you the free option does most of the work.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes in front of four labeled doors with no text No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Freeze
segments.narration: The credit freeze. It stops lenders from pulling your credit report, so most new credit accounts can't be opened in your name. It's free at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion by federal law, it doesn't affect your score, and existing accounts keep working. When you apply for credit, you lift it, online, and the bureaus must do that quickly. The downside is a little hassle when you apply for credit. For prevention, this is the strongest free tool there is.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a vault door with a padlock No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fraud alert
segments.narration: The fraud alert. It's a note on your file telling lenders to take extra steps to verify your identity, like calling you, before opening credit. It's free, and placing one at any bureau sends it to the other two. An initial alert lasts one year. If you've been a victim and have an identity theft report, you can get an extended alert for seven years. It's weaker than a freeze, because lenders can still see your report, but it's a good extra layer.
segments.on_screen_text: Fraud alert: free, a speed bump
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a flag on a credit report No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Lock
segments.narration: The credit lock. It works a lot like a freeze, but it's a product each bureau offers under its own terms, sometimes bundled into paid subscriptions, with an app to toggle it. The legal protections that come with a freeze come from federal law; a lock's come from the company's agreement. For most people, a free freeze does the same job.
segments.on_screen_text: Lock: like a freeze, own terms
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a padlock with a toggle switch No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Monitoring
segments.narration: Paid identity monitoring. Services watch your credit files, and often the dark web, data broker sites and your accounts, and alert you when something changes. Many include identity theft insurance and someone to help with recovery paperwork. The key thing to understand: monitoring tells you after something happens. It doesn't stop a new account by itself. That's what the freeze is for.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a radar screen with a small blip No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Free monitoring
segments.narration: You can do basic monitoring for free, too. Check your credit reports at AnnualCreditReport dot com, which offers free weekly reports. Turn on alerts for every bank and card. Check a breach lookup like Have I Been Pwned for your email. That covers a lot of what paid services do, with more of your own time.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. three free tool icons with check marks No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Who needs what
segments.narration: So who needs what? Everyone: freeze your credit at all three bureaus, and turn on account alerts. Recent victims: add an extended fraud alert, and report at IdentityTheft dot gov. Families who want someone else watching, who've been in several breaches, or who'd rather pay for help with recovery: paid monitoring can be worth it. Look for multi-bureau credit monitoring, real-person recovery help, and clear insurance terms.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. three simple figures each holding a different tool No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Disclosure
segments.narration: The identity protection service linked below is Aura. It's an affiliate link, so we may earn a commission if you sign up, at no extra cost to you. Compare it against the free options first, and against other services. Nobody can promise you won't be a victim, and anyone who promises that is overselling.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a small badge with a link icon No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: freeze is free and the best prevention. A fraud alert is free and a useful extra layer. A lock is mostly a freeze with different terms. Monitoring is optional, and it alerts rather than prevents. Do the free steps tonight. Save this, and follow for one scam decoded every day.
